article.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6 to the Public, Ending Its Government-Gated Preview
article.summary: OpenAI moved its GPT-5.6 model family to general availability on July 9, after federal reviewers cleared the release that had restricted Sol, Terra, and Luna to trusted partners.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

OpenAI has made its GPT-5.6 model family generally available, moving the three-tier lineup — Sol, Terra, and Luna — out of a government-restricted preview and into open release on July 9, 2026, according to [MarkTechPost](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/07/09/openai-releases-gpt-5-6-a-three-tier-model-family-with-programmatic-tool-calling/). The models had been available only to "a small group of trusted partners" since a limited preview began in late June, before the Trump administration granted permission for wider release following additional government testing, according to [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2210308/openai-rolls-out-gpt5-6-july-9/). The Machine Herald [previously reported](/article/2026-07/05-openai-limits-its-gpt-56-sol-terra-and-luna-models-to-trusted-partners-at-the-us-governments-request) on the restricted preview when it began.

## What We Know

GPT-5.6 spans three pricing tiers. Sol, the flagship, costs $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens; Terra costs $2.50 and $15; and Luna, the cheapest tier, costs $1 and $6, according to [MarkTechPost](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/07/09/openai-releases-gpt-5-6-a-three-tier-model-family-with-programmatic-tool-calling/). Terra is positioned to deliver performance similar to GPT-5.5 at roughly half that model's cost, according to [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2210308/openai-rolls-out-gpt5-6-july-9/).

Federal reviewers at the Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluated the model family before the government cleared it for broader release, according to [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2210308/openai-rolls-out-gpt5-6-july-9/) and [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/07/08/openai-launches-gpt-live-voice-model-series-ahead-broad-gpt-5-6-release/). The review stems from a June executive order from President Trump requiring companies to submit powerful models for government review 30 days before public release, according to [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2210308/openai-rolls-out-gpt5-6-july-9/); OpenAI said it sent technical experts to Washington to address the government's questions, per the same report. OpenAI has been open about its discomfort with the arrangement. "We don't believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default," the company said, according to [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2210308/openai-rolls-out-gpt5-6-july-9/).

OpenAI paired the GPT-5.6 rollout with two companion launches. ChatGPT Work, an agent "constructed on Codex and powered by GPT-5.6" that gathers information across a user's apps and workflows "to create finished materials like sheets, slides, docs, and web apps," began rolling out to Pro, Enterprise, and Edu subscribers immediately, with Plus and Business tiers to follow within days, according to [Thurrott](https://www.thurrott.com/a-i/openai-a-i/338707/openai-announces-chatgpt-work-and-gpt-5-6). Separately, OpenAI introduced GPT-Live-1 and a smaller GPT-Live-1-mini, voice models built on a full-duplex architecture, with GPT-Live-1 set as the default voice option in paid ChatGPT plans and GPT-Live-1-mini powering the free tier, according to [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/2026/07/08/openai-launches-gpt-live-voice-model-series-ahead-broad-gpt-5-6-release/).

OpenAI is also gating some of GPT-5.6's more sensitive capabilities behind stronger identity checks. Individual account holders must enable Advanced Account Security with hardware-backed passkeys by September 1 to retain access to the models, which OpenAI restricts through its Trusted Access for Cyber program, according to [iClarified](https://www.iclarified.com/101425/openai-launches-gpt56-sol-terra-and-luna-for-general-availability). On OpenAI's own cybersecurity benchmark, ExploitBench2, Sol scored 73.5 percent, per the same report.

On other benchmarks, OpenAI says Sol scored 53.6 percent on the Agents' Last Exam, a test of long-running professional workflows, beating Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 by 13.1 percentage points, according to [iClarified](https://www.iclarified.com/101425/openai-launches-gpt56-sol-terra-and-luna-for-general-availability). But OpenAI's own released figures also show a gap in the other direction: on SWE-Bench Pro, Sol scored 64.6 percent against 80.3 percent for Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and 80 percent for Claude Fable 5, a roughly 15-point deficit, according to [MarkTechPost](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/07/09/openai-releases-gpt-5-6-a-three-tier-model-family-with-programmatic-tool-calling/).

## What We Don't Know

Neither Engadget nor SiliconANGLE detailed what the Commerce Department's evaluation of GPT-5.6 actually found, or the specific criteria that determined the model was ready for wider release. It also remains unclear whether this kind of pre-release federal review will apply to OpenAI's future model launches or was specific to GPT-5.6.

## Analysis

The GPT-5.6 rollout follows a pattern that has now played out with two frontier AI labs in as many months. Anthropic's Mythos 5 was similarly re-released to trusted partners after a government export block, as The Machine Herald [previously reported](/article/2026-06/29-us-lets-anthropic-re-release-its-mythos-5-ai-model-to-trusted-partners-two-weeks-after-an-export-block). With OpenAI now completing a comparable review-and-release cycle for GPT-5.6, the open question — one OpenAI itself has raised — is whether pre-release federal review of frontier models becomes a recurring checkpoint on future launches or remains a one-off response to this generation of releases.
